client: I've been dreading the family reunion this weekend. Ever since my grandma passed, being around everyone just makes me feel empty and disconnected. I know they're trying to be supportive, but it just reminds me how much I miss her and how nothing feels the same anymore.
therapist:
It sounds like this reunion is bringing up deep feelings of loss and loneliness, especially without your grandma there. That empty, disconnected feeling makes complete sense when you're grieving someone so important.  

What thoughts come up when you imagine being with your family this weekend? Do you notice any expectations about how you "should" feel or act?

client: I keep thinking about how my grandma would have been the one to make me feel welcome and included at these gatherings. Now I just feel like an outsider, like I don't really belong there without her. Part of me thinks I should be "over it" by now since she passed two years ago, but the pain still feels so fresh.
therapist:
It sounds like you're holding two painful thoughts at once - missing your grandma's comforting presence, and judging yourself for still grieving deeply. Grief doesn't follow a timeline, and two years isn't very long when you've lost someone so central to your sense of belonging.  

What would it feel like to let go of that "should" about being "over it"? How might that change your experience of the reunion?

client:
I know logically that grief doesn't have a timeline, but I still feel embarrassed when people ask how I'm doing and I get choked up. My cousins seem to have moved on, and I worry they'll think I'm being dramatic if I can't keep it together at the reunion. 

The idea of letting go of the "should" sounds nice in theory, but I don't know how to actually do that when everyone else expects me to be okay by now. What if trying to accept my feelings just makes me cry more in front of everyone?
therapist:
It makes complete sense that you'd feel self-conscious when others seem to have moved forward while your grief still feels so present. That fear of being judged as "dramatic" adds another heavy layer to an already painful experience.  

What if, instead of focusing on whether you cry, we explore what it would be like to give yourself permission to feel whatever arises in the moment? How might that shift your relationship with these emotions?

client:
I get what you're saying about giving myself permission to feel, but it's not that simple. When I start crying in public, I can see people getting uncomfortable or looking at me like I'm being too much. That just makes me feel worse and more isolated. 

The idea of letting myself feel whatever comes up sounds nice in theory, but I'm scared I'll completely lose control if I do that. What if the emotions just overwhelm me and I can't stop crying once I start?
therapist:
It sounds like there's a real fear that if you let the tears come, they might feel endless—like opening a floodgate you can't close. That fear of losing control in front of others makes perfect sense, especially when you're already feeling so tender.  

What would it feel like to plan small moments of privacy during the reunion—maybe stepping outside for a few breaths—so you can honor your emotions without worrying about others' reactions?

client:
I get what you're saying about planning moments to step away, but I'm worried people will notice and think I'm being weird or antisocial. My family already makes comments about me being "too sensitive" and I don't want to give them more reasons to judge me. 

The idea of letting myself cry even in private scares me because what if I can't stop before going back inside? I've had panic attacks where once I start crying, it spirals and I can't pull myself together.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two fears—the worry about being judged for stepping away, and the fear of being overwhelmed by emotions if you don't. That's an incredibly difficult spot to be in, especially when your family's comments have made you feel like your sensitivity is something to hide.  

What if we explored one small, manageable way to soothe yourself in those moments—like a grounding technique you could use discreetly, even in the bathroom? Would that feel safer than risking a full emotional release?

client:
I get what you're saying, but I'm not sure grounding techniques would help. When I'm in those family situations, my mind just races with all the things I "should" be doing, and taking a break makes me feel even guiltier. 

Also, what if someone notices I disappeared to the bathroom? They'll probably think I'm being dramatic or weak. I don't want to give them more reasons to judge me.
therapist:
It sounds like every possible path feels unsafe right now—staying present risks being overwhelmed, stepping away triggers guilt, and even small acts of self-care feel like they might backfire. That’s an exhausting place to be, especially when you’re already carrying so much grief.  

I’m hearing that judgment from your family adds another layer of pain to an already tender wound. What would it feel like to acknowledge—just to yourself—that their inability to hold space for your grief says more about *them* than it does about you? You don’t have to believe it yet, but what if we just planted that seed?

client:
I hear what you're saying, but it's hard not to take their reactions personally. When they criticize how I'm grieving, it just reinforces this voice in my head that says I'm doing everything wrong.  

The idea that it's about them and not me... I want to believe that, but right now it just makes me feel even more alone. Like if they can't understand me, who will?
therapist:
That loneliness cuts deep—when the people who *should* understand you the most make you feel like your pain is a burden or a flaw. That voice saying you're "doing everything wrong" must feel so heavy when it's echoing their words back to you.  

I wonder if we could sit with this feeling of aloneness for a moment—not to fix it, but to acknowledge how real and valid it is. What does this loneliness *need* right now, if it had a voice? Not what others think it *should* need, but what *your* heart is truly asking for?  

(We can stay right here with this ache—you don’t have to rush toward solutions when the hurt needs to be heard first.)

client:
It’s just... I don’t even know what it needs. Maybe just to not feel like a problem that needs fixing all the time? But when I try to tell people that, they either give me clichés or just look uncomfortable. It makes me feel like I’m broken in a way that’s too messy for them to handle.  

And the worst part is, I start believing it—that I *am* too much. Like my loneliness is some kind of failure on my part.
therapist:
That belief—that you're "too much"—sounds like it's taken root so deeply that it's become a lens for how you see yourself in every interaction. It's heartbreaking to hear how isolated you feel, especially when reaching out for understanding only seems to confirm that belief.  

What if we gently challenged that idea together? When you say you're "too messy," I wonder... could that actually be a sign of how deeply you *loved* your grandma, rather than a failure? Grief isn't tidy—it's the price of a bond that mattered.  

(We can stay right here with this, too. No need to rush—your feelings aren't an emergency to solve.)

client:
I get what you're saying about grief not being tidy, but I still feel like I should be handling it better by now. It's been months, and I see other people move on while I'm still crying at random moments. That just proves I'm too much, doesn't it? 

The idea that my messiness shows how much I loved her... that's nice, but it doesn't change how exhausting I must be for everyone around me. My friends have stopped asking how I'm doing because I know they're tired of my sadness.
therapist:
It sounds like you're measuring your grief against others' and finding yourself coming up short—but what if that comparison itself is part of the pain? The truth is, your tears aren't proof you're "too much," but proof that your love for your grandma doesn't just vanish because time passes.  

I hear how exhausting it feels to worry about burdening others with your sadness. But might there be a middle ground—where you could honor your grief *and* gently challenge the belief that it makes you unlovable? What would that look like to you?

client:
I get what you're saying about not comparing grief, but it's hard when everyone else seems to have moved on. My family talks about grandma like it's just happy memories now, but I still wake up crying sometimes.  

I guess the middle ground would be letting myself feel sad without panicking that people will get tired of me, but... how do you even know when you're being "too much"? Last time I tried opening up, my friend changed the subject really fast.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between two painful realities—your grief still feeling so raw while others seem to have shifted to reminiscing, and the fear that expressing your sadness will push people away. That double bind makes it so hard to trust your own emotional needs.  

When your friend changed the subject, that must have felt like confirmation of your fears. But I wonder: could we explore what *you* need in those moments when others can't meet you where you are? Not to fix the grief, but to care for yourself *in* it?
